applied.problem: Two claims are absolute where the research hedges: a damaged sheath does not always trip the test (one study finds cases with no current despite damage), and water in the sheath can promote water trees rather than always growing them.

The mistake 'Using 10 kV on every sheath, whatever its thickness' contradicts the practice's own rule of thumb and a cited offshore spec that uses a flat 10 kV; it is a mistake only when the spec asks for 4 kV per mm.
The trap calls a flat 10 kV on every sheath wrong, yet the same card says other specs use other levels and one offshore spec asks for a flat 10 kV; it is a slip only under the 4 kV per mm rule.

Screen 2 says water in the sheath grows water trees until the insulation fails, stated as certain where the research says moisture and field can promote them; screen 3's 'a new sheath takes 8 kV per mm' omits that the factory routine test may be a spark test instead.
